  • profile - produce the profiles YAML file
  • apply - build indices from the generated definition files

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Compress the shards of a registry.

USAGE

kmhelpers compress [OPTIONS]
Argument Description -r, --registry-path DIR Path to kmindex registry (required) --sh, --shard PATTERN Shards to compress, as names or glob patterns, repeatable or comma-separated (default: all)

I/O

Input: kmindex registry (-r), shards (--shard, default: all) Output: compressed shards in place within the registry

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description --block-size INT Size of uncompressed blocks in MB (default: 8) --cpr-level INT Compression level 1–22 (default: 3) --reorder Enable column reordering before compression -s, --sampling INT Number of rows to sample for column reordering (default: 20000) --column-per-block INT Reorder columns in groups of N (0 = all columns, must be multiple of 8; default: 0) -t, --threads INT Number of threads (default: 14) --delete Delete the uncompressed matrices after successful compression --check Check query results after compression

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Compresses each selected shard with kmindex compress, one after the other. Without --shard, every shard of the registry is compressed. A pattern that matches no shard is a warning; the command fails only if no shard matches. A failed shard does not stop the others: the command fails at the end and lists them.

Column reordering - use --reorder to reorder columns before compression, which can improve compression ratio. Use --sampling to control how many rows are sampled to determine the optimal column order.

Deletion - use --delete to remove the uncompressed matrices after successful compression. Requires confirmation unless -Y is passed at the root level.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Compress every shard of the registry
kmhelpers compress -r ./registry

# Compress the shards of one group
kmhelpers compress -r ./registry --sh 'my_index_g0_*'

# With column reordering
kmhelpers compress -r ./registry --sh my_index --reorder -s 50000

# Custom compression level with multiple threads
kmhelpers compress -r ./registry --sh my_index --cpr-level 6 -t 16

# Delete uncompressed index after compression
kmhelpers compress -r ./registry --sh my_index --delete

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Scan a directory or import a sample list, then run the full list → profile → compose pipeline in a single command.

USAGE

kmhelpers design -o DESIGN_DIR -n NAME [-s SESSION] [OPTIONS] INPUT
Argument Description INPUT Directory to scan, a plain-text / YAML sample list, or an existing JSONL sample index (required) -o, --output-dir DESIGN_DIR Output directory (required) -n, --name NAME Name of the created index (required) -s, --session SESSION Session name: subdirectory of DESIGN_DIR/compose/NAME/ and tag appended to index names (default: timestamp YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS) -k, --kmer-size INT K-mer size for counting (default: 25) --dt, --data-type TEXT Data type: a/assembled (default) or u/unassembled (raw reads)

I/O

Input: directory to scan, a plain-text / YAML sample list, or a JSONL sample index (.jsonl, in which case the list step is skipped and INPUT is used as-is) Output (pass to build, plan or apply): DESIGN_DIR itself, with -s SESSION (default: the last session); the session is DESIGN_DIR/compose/NAME/SESSION/index.yaml Intermediate files (reused by later runs, not passed to build):

  • DESIGN_DIR/list/samples_SESSION.jsonl - sample manifest, read by the session's shards (not copied)
  • DESIGN_DIR/profile/ - span profile (profile.yaml, baseline.csv, groups.png)
  • DESIGN_DIR/compose/NAME/layout.yaml - layout reused by updates

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
DESIGN_DIR/                            -> INPUT of build/plan/apply (-s SESSION)
├── list/
│   └── samples_SESSION.jsonl          sample manifest, read by the session (omitted if INPUT is already a JSONL index)
├── profile/
│   ├── profile.yaml                   intermediate: span profile (input for compose)
│   ├── baseline.csv                   intermediate: natural distribution
│   └── groups.png                     distribution plot
└── compose/                           COMPOSE_DIR
    └── NAME/                          the index
        ├── layout.yaml                state of the index: groups, shard budget, shards, partitions, bitw, sessions
        └── SESSION/
            ├── index.yaml             the session: parameters, size and shards (readable summary)
            ├── summary.csv            one row per shard
            └── shards/
                └── NAME_g<i>_p<k>.yaml  the samples this session adds to shard NAME_g<i>_p<k>

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
Pass the index definition file to build:

kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db -n coli -s initial
kmhelpers build coli_db -o coli_build

Set -s to get a predictable path. Without it, SESSION is a timestamp: design logs the exact build command at the end of the run, or look up the folder in DESIGN_DIR/compose/NAME/. See build - Paths for the full directory layout.

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description -g, --group N Partition Bloom Filters into N storage-balanced groups and overlay on plot; 0 chooses N (default: 0): one group when the built index takes at most 4 GB, else as profile -g 0. Tuned by the KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_* environment variables, see profile - Grouping --ngp, --no-grouping One group, no grouping strategy: every sample gets the Bloom filter of the largest one; not with -g N -b, --base FLOAT Base for span bucket boundaries (default: 1.1) --sb, --shard-budget INT Shard budget: a shard of span s holds at most ceil8(budget / base^s) samples (default: 2**43 for a new index); 0 for no limit, see compose --fp, --false-positive-rate FLOAT Target Bloom-filter false-positive rate (default: 0.25) -P, --partition-count INT Hidden. Fix the partition count of every shard for the life of the index: inherited by every later session, no longer adapted to the system limits of plan/build. 0 (default) lets the first plan of each shard size it, see compose - Partitioning --minim-size INT Minimizer size (4-15), fixed for the life of the index (default: 10 for a new index, the layout's value on an update) --ab, --abundance-bits INT Build an abundance index with N bits per cell (2^N abundance classes); 0 builds a presence/absence index (default: 0), see compose --nc, --no-count Skip k-mer counting with ntcard --kr, --kmer-ratio FLOAT Multiply the k-mer ratio (k-mer occurrences per counted k-mer) that sizes the build memory (default: 1), see compose - Partitioning --ncl, --no-copy-list With a JSONL INPUT, point the index definition files to it instead of copying it into the compose output folder; the list must then stay in place and unchanged as it is used for building. A list written by design is never copied --shard-budget-bytes SIZE Hidden. Cap a shard by its size on disk (e.g. 10GB) rather than by --shard-budget: when set, --shard-budget is not used. Cannot be combined with --shard-budget, see compose --lg, --leaf-grouping Group files by leaf folder; each leaf directory becomes one sample -p, --paired [REGEX] Group mate files (R1/R2) of a directory into one sample, see list -a, --autorename Rename duplicate sample IDs by appending a numeric suffix instead of skipping --ntt, --ntcard-threads INT Number of threads for ntcard k-mer counting (default: 8)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
design chains list, profile, and compose into a single invocation. It is equivalent to running the three commands in sequence with the intermediate files automatically routed between steps.

Step 1 - list: scans INPUT recursively for sequence files (or imports a sample list), counts k-mers with ntcard, and writes a JSONL manifest to DESIGN_DIR/list/. This step is skipped if INPUT is already a JSONL sample index (.jsonl); it is used directly as the manifest for the remaining steps.

Step 2 - profile: reads k-mer counts from the manifest, assigns each sample to a Bloom-filter span, computes a storage-balanced grouping, and writes profile.yaml, baseline.csv, and groups.png to DESIGN_DIR/profile/. This step is skipped automatically if a layout file already exists at DESIGN_DIR/compose/NAME/layout.yaml (re-run scenario).

Groups - with -g 0, design keeps one group when the built index takes at most 4 GB: profile compares its presence/absence sizes with 4 GB / bitw (1.33 GB with --ab 3). Larger indexes are grouped as profile -g 0 does. KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_SINGLE_MAX changes the 4 GB (0 turns the rule off), -g N forces N groups, and --no-grouping keeps one group whatever the size.

Step 3 - compose: reads the manifest and the profile to generate the index definition file DESIGN_DIR/compose/NAME/SESSION/index.yaml.

Updates - if the compose layout file already exists from a previous run, the profile step is skipped and the existing layout is used directly. This allows re-running design with a new -s to add samples to an existing index without re-profiling, then building the new session into the same BUILD_DIR. The new session is merged with the existing index at build time, which keeps both versions on disk - see build - Updating an index.

False-positive rate - a higher rate reduces Bloom-filter size and disk footprint. At query time the findere algorithm compensates by querying \((k+z)\)-mers, reducing the effective FP rate to \(p^z\). Recommended: build with --fp 0.25 (default), query with -z 6, giving \(0.25^6 \approx 0.024\,\%\) effective FP rate.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Full pipeline from a directory, then build
kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db -n coli -s initial
kmhelpers build coli_db -o coli_build

# Add new samples to the same index, then build into the same BUILD_DIR
kmhelpers design /data/new_sequences -o coli_db -n coli -s update
kmhelpers build coli_db -s update -o coli_build

# Skip k-mer counting (if counts are already in the sample list)
kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db -n coli --no-count

# Group files by leaf folder
kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db -n coli --leaf-grouping

# Custom k-mer size and false-positive rate
kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db -n coli -k 31 --fp 0.1

# Force a specific partition count
kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db -n coli -P 4

# Abundance index of paired raw reads (4 abundance classes)
kmhelpers design /data/reads -o reads_db -n reads --dt u --paired --ab 2

# Import from a plain-text file list
kmhelpers design my_files.txt -o coli_db -n coli

# Re-use an existing JSONL sample index, skipping the list step
kmhelpers design coli_db/list/samples_20260101_120000.jsonl -o coli_db -n coli

  • compose - compose step only

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Download and install kmtricks, kmindex and ntcard prebuilt binaries from their GitHub releases.

USAGE

kmhelpers install-deps [OPTIONS]

I/O

Input: none (downloads from github.com/tlemane/kmtricks, github.com/tlemane/kmindex and github.com/sebllns/ntCard) Output: kmtricks, kmindex, kmindex-server and ntcard binaries in the installation directory

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --kmtricks VERSION kmtricks version to install, 0 to skip (default: 1.6.0) --kmindex VERSION kmindex version to install, 0 to skip (default: 0.6.1) --ntcard VERSION ntcard release tag to install, 0 to skip (default: 1.2.2-portable1) --target [x86_64\|arm64] Target architecture (default: detected from the current machine) --path DIR Installation directory (default: directory of the kmhelpers executable)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The operating system (Linux or macOS) is detected automatically. Existing binaries with the same name are overwritten after confirmation (skipped with the global -Y option). A warning is logged if the installation directory is not in PATH.

ntcard comes from sebllns/ntCard, a fork of ntCard that publishes portable builds: fully static on Linux, and depending only on the system library on macOS. The download is verified against the SHA256SUMS file of the release.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Install default versions next to kmhelpers
kmhelpers install-deps

# Install only kmindex 0.6.1 into a custom directory
kmhelpers -Y install-deps --kmtricks 0 --kmindex 0.6.1 --path ~/bin

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Scan a directory or import a sample list, count k-mers, and produce a JSONL sample manifest.

USAGE

kmhelpers list [OPTIONS] INPUT
Argument Description INPUT Directory to scan, or a plain-text / YAML sample list (required) - see Input formats -o, --output FILE Path for the output JSONL file (required) -k, --kmer-size INT K-mer size for counting (default: 25) --dt, --data-type TEXT Data type: a/assembled (default) or u/unassembled (raw reads) - see K-mer counting

I/O

Input: directory to scan, or a plain-text / YAML sample list Output: JSONL sample manifest (-o)

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description --nc, --no-count Skip k-mer counting with ntcard --lg, --leaf-grouping Group files by leaf folder; each leaf directory becomes one sample -p, --paired [REGEX] Group mate files (R1/R2) of a directory into one sample, see Grouping -c, --continue Resume from an existing output file, skipping already-listed samples -a, --autorename Rename duplicate sample IDs by appending a numeric suffix instead of skipping --ntt, --ntcard-threads INT Number of threads for ntcard k-mer counting (default: 8)

docs.title: Plain text (.txt)
docs.text:
One sample per line. Lines starting with # and empty lines are ignored.

# [sample_id] file_1[,file_2,...] [kmer_count]
sample_A  /data/sample_A_1.fa,/data/sample_A_2.fa  1234567
sample_B  /data/sample_B.fa
/data/sample_C.fa
  • sample_id is optional - if omitted, it is derived from the first filename (without extension)
  • Multiple files for one sample are comma-separated
  • kmer_count is optional - if omitted and --no-count is not set, it will be computed

docs.title: YAML (.yaml / .yml)
docs.text:
k: 25
assembled: true
samples:
  sample_A:
    files:
      - /data/sample_A_1.fa
      - /data/sample_A_2.fa
    kmer_count: 1234567
  sample_B:
    files:
      - /data/sample_B.fa

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
INPUT can be a directory (scanned recursively for sequence files) or a sample list file (plain text or YAML) - the type is detected automatically. K-mer counts are parsed or computed for each sample and written to the JSONL manifest.

Grouping - by default, each file is treated as its own sample. Use --leaf-grouping to group files by leaf folder, where each leaf directory becomes one sample whose ID is the folder name.

Paired reads - use --paired to group mate files into one sample. The last match of a regex is removed from each file name (without extension), and files of the same directory with the same result form one sample named after it. The default regex [._][Rr]?[12](?=[._]|$) matches mate tokens such as _R1, _R2, _1, .2:

  • S1_R1_clean.fastq.gz + S1_R2_clean.fastq.gz -> S1_clean
  • SRR123_1.fq.gz + SRR123_2.fq.gz -> SRR123

Files without a mate token stay single-file samples. Pass a custom regex as --paired=REGEX (the = is required when another argument follows). Without --paired, a warning is logged when unassembled files (--dt u) look like read pairs. --paired cannot be combined with --leaf-grouping.

K-mer counting - enabled by default. Counting is skipped for any sample that already has a kmer_count value. Use --no-count to skip counting entirely. The --data-type option controls what is counted:

  • assembled (default) - counts all distinct k-mers; suited for assemblies where every k-mer is expected at least once
  • unassembled - counts only k-mers appearing at least twice, filtering out likely sequencing errors; suited for raw reads

The same ntcard run also records kmer_total, the k-mer occurrences of the sample, which sizes the build memory (see compose - Partitioning).

Resuming - if the output file already exists, it is backed up. Pass --continue to resume from that backup without reprocessing already-listed samples; otherwise the run starts fresh. Use --autorename to rename duplicate sample IDs instead of skipping them.

Top-level keys other than samples are written as-is into the output header.

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
The output is a JSONL file. The first line is a header and the remaining lines are one sample per line:

{"k": 25, "assembled": true}
{"name": "sample_A", "files": ["/data/sequences/sample_A/reads_1.fa", "/data/sequences/sample_A/reads_2.fa"], "kmer_count": 1234567, "kmer_total": 1302114}
{"name": "sample_B", "files": ["/data/sequences/sample_B/reads.fa"], "kmer_count": 987654, "kmer_total": 1011540}

This file is the input for profile and compose.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Basic scan, one file per sample
kmhelpers list /data/sequences -o samples.jsonl

# Group files by leaf folder
kmhelpers list /data/sequences -o samples.jsonl --leaf-grouping

# Group paired-end reads (R1/R2) into one sample per pair
kmhelpers list /data/reads -o samples.jsonl --dt u --paired

# Custom mate pattern, e.g. "sample.fwd.fq" / "sample.rev.fq"
kmhelpers list /data/reads -o samples.jsonl --dt u --paired='\.(fwd|rev)$'

# Custom k-mer size
kmhelpers list /data/sequences -o samples.jsonl -k 31

# Skip k-mer counting
kmhelpers list /data/sequences -o samples.jsonl --no-count

# Import from a plain-text file list
kmhelpers list my_files.txt -o samples.jsonl

# Import from a YAML sample list
kmhelpers list my_files.yaml -o samples.jsonl

# Resume an interrupted run without reprocessing already-listed samples
kmhelpers list /data/sequences -o samples.jsonl -c

# Rename duplicate sample IDs instead of skipping them
kmhelpers list /data/sequences -o samples.jsonl -a

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
K-mer counting relies on ntcard, which is automatically installed as a dependency when installing kmhelpers via conda.

Hamid Mohamadi, Hamza Khan, and Inanc Birol. ntCard: a streaming algorithm for cardinality estimation in genomics data. Bioinformatics (2017) 33 (9): 1324–1330. 10.1093/bioinformatics/btw832

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• profile - produce the profiles YAML file
  • compose - use the JSONL output to compose index definitions

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Manage k-mer index registries.

USAGE

kmhelpers manage [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
Argument Description -r, --registry-path DIR Path to kmindex registry (default: current directory)

I/O

Input: kmindex registry (-r), subcommand-specific arguments Output: updated registry state (create, add, remove, rename, relink) or printed info (list, info, check)

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text: Subcommand Description create Initialise a registry and optionally register existing indices add Register existing kmtricks indices in an existing registry list List all indices in a registry info Show detailed information about an index check Validate registry consistency and index structures remove Remove one or more indices from the registry rename Rename an index relink Recreate links after moving index files

docs.title: create
docs.text: Option Description -i, --input-dir DIR Directory containing existing kmtricks indices to register --sh, --shard TEXT Shard(s) to register (default: all found)

docs.title: add
docs.text: Option Description -i, --input-dir DIR Directory containing kmtricks indices to add (required) --sh, --shard TEXT Shard(s) to register (default: all found)

docs.title: check
docs.text: Option Description --sh, --shard TEXT Check only these shards (repeatable, default: all); fails if one is not registered -v, --verbose Show detailed validation output

docs.title: info
docs.text: Option Description --sh, --shard TEXT Shard to show information for (required) --json Output as JSON

docs.title: remove
docs.text: Option Description --sh, --shard TEXT Shard(s) to remove (required, repeatable) -d, --delete-files Also delete index files from disk -y, --yes Skip confirmation prompt --missing-ok Skip index IDs that are not registered instead of failing --keep-link Only edit index.json: leave a symlinked entry in place

docs.title: rename
docs.text: Option Description -f, --from TEXT Current index ID (required) -t, --to TEXT New index ID (required)

docs.title: relink
docs.text: Option Description -i, --input-dir DIR Directory containing the moved index files (required) --sh, --shard TEXT Shard to relink (default: all registered shards)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Create a registry in the current directory
kmhelpers manage create

# Create a registry and register indices from a directory
kmhelpers manage create -i /data/indices

# List all registered indices
kmhelpers manage list
kmhelpers manage -r /path/to/registry list

# Add indices from a directory to an existing registry
kmhelpers manage add -i /data/new_indices

# Show info for a specific index
kmhelpers manage info --sh my_index

# Show info as JSON
kmhelpers manage info --sh my_index --json

# Check consistency
kmhelpers manage check

# Remove an index (keep files)
kmhelpers manage remove --sh my_index

# Remove an index and delete files from disk
kmhelpers manage remove --sh my_index -d

# Remove multiple indices without confirmation
kmhelpers manage remove --sh idx1 --sh idx2 -y

# Rename an index
kmhelpers manage rename -f old_name -t new_name

# Relink all indices from a new directory
kmhelpers manage relink -i /new/location

# Relink a specific index
kmhelpers manage relink -i /new/location --sh my_index

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Run a sequence of commands defined in a YAML pipeline file.

USAGE

kmhelpers pipeline [OPTIONS] PIPELINE_FILE
Argument Description PIPELINE_FILE YAML pipeline definition file (required)

I/O

Input: YAML pipeline definition file Output: depends on pipeline steps

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description -x KEY VALUE Override a parameter for all steps (repeatable)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
pipeline executes a series of kmhelpers commands in order, as defined in a YAML file. Steps run sequentially. Use -x to override parameters for all steps at runtime.

Priority - global config (-C) < pipeline YAML < -x overrides.

docs.title: Dict format (simple, no repeated commands)
docs.text:
compose:
  workdir: /path/to/workdir
  input_files: [samples.yaml]
build:
  workdir: /path/to/workdir
  threads: 8

docs.title: List format (allows repeating the same command)
docs.text:
- apply:
    workdir: /path/a
    input_files: [a.yaml]
- apply:
    workdir: /path/b
    input_files: [b.yaml]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Run a pipeline
kmhelpers pipeline my_pipeline.yaml

# Override workdir and threads for all steps
kmhelpers pipeline my_pipeline.yaml -x workdir /tmp -x threads 16

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Decide how to build the indices of a definition file, and write the plan: plan.yaml and the scripts of every shard, which apply runs.

USAGE

kmhelpers plan [OPTIONS] INPUT
Argument Description INPUT The design directory (DESIGN_DIR of design), a compose directory or one of its indexes (COMPOSE_DIR/NAME), a session (COMPOSE_DIR/NAME/SESSION or its index.yaml), or one shard file (SESSION/shards/<shard>.yaml, built without merge) (required) -s, --session SESSION Session to use when INPUT is a directory (default: the last one composed) -o, --output-dir BUILD_DIR Index directory the plan targets, same as for build and apply (required)

I/O

Input: DESIGN_DIR of design (or COMPOSE_DIR of compose), with -s to pick a session; it resolves to compose/NAME/SESSION/index.yaml (see design - Next Step) Output: BUILD_DIR/assets/SESSION/plan.yaml, one directory of scripts per shard (BUILD_DIR/assets/SESSION/<shard>/), with --cluster the SLURM files (BUILD_DIR/assets/SESSION/slurm/), report in BUILD_DIR/logs/ (see build - Report)

See build - Paths for the directory layout.

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description --bp, --base-path DIR Base path to resolve relative sample paths --sh, --shard TEXT Shards to plan, as names or glob patterns (repeatable or comma-separated, e.g. idx_g0_p1, 'idx_g0_*'); a part name (<shard>_<session>) plans that part as its own index --cpj, --chunks-per-job INT Chunks of a shard one job builds: 0 (default) for one job per shard, its chunks then its merge; else jobs <shard>_j<k> of up to N chunks, then a job <shard>_merge (see Jobs) --hpc, --cluster FILE YAML file of the scheduler and the resources of each kind of job: sizes the plan from them (instead of --limits) and writes the SLURM files (see Cluster) --threads INT Hidden. Force the number of kmtricks threads instead of sizing them from --limits --ncp, --skip-compression Skip compression of intermediate files during index building (useful on slow disks) --limits JSON Resource limits used to auto-size threads/partitions when --threads is not set, for the shard's k-mer occurrences (see compose - Partitioning) (ram, files, threads), and the inputs of one merge (ram, files, maps = vm.max_map_count); see build - Builds and merges --safety-margin FLOAT Fraction of a detected system limit, or of a --cluster job's memory, to use (default: 0.9) --max-chunks INT Max number of kmtricks chunks a shard is built in; bigger chunks mean fewer build/merge passes but fewer threads. 0 disables the cap (default: 64) --cb, --chunk-budget INT K-mer budget of one kmtricks chunk: a chunk of span s holds at most ceil8(budget / base^s) samples. 0 for no limit (default: 2**37), see build - Shards and chunks -x, --fail-fast Abort on first failure instead of continuing --keep-previous Keep the replaced version of an updated index in BUILD_DIR/work/SESSION/previous/ instead of deleting it --off, --offline Skip local path validation (useful when exporting scripts for another machine)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
plan validates all sample paths of the session and takes every build decision: partitions, threads, chunks, merges and jobs, from the resource limits and the registry as it is. It builds nothing and touches no registry. apply then runs the plan as it is: it has no sizing option.

BUILD_DIR/assets/SESSION/
  plan.yaml                     the plan (below)
  slurm/                        with --cluster
  <shard>/
    <part>.sh, <part>.fof       one script per kmtricks run (or <part>_chunk<N>.sh)
    merge.sh                    the merge of the shard: check, merge, publish, check, clean
    merge/                      the run list and the inputs of each merge step

A shard directory is emptied and rewritten each time it is planned. Every script can be run again after an interruption: a run script does nothing when its samples are already published or its run is complete, and deletes and rebuilds an incomplete run.

plan.yaml - one task per part (<shard>_<session>): one session's samples added to one shard.

type: plan
kmhelpers: 0.8.0
definition: /db/compose/idx/initial/index.yaml
fingerprint: {files: {<input file>: <sha256>, ...}}
options: {limits: {...}, chunks_per_job: 3, ...}
tasks:
  idx_g0_initial:
    shard: idx_g0             # the index in BUILD_DIR
    dir: idx_g0/
    samples: 448
    partitions: 64
    minim_size: 10
    threads: 24
    chunks: {idx_g0_initial_chunk0: {samples: 64}, ...}
    merge:
      script: merge.sh
      expects: {registered: false, samples: 0}   # the registry as plan saw it
      mode: merge             # move: a single run and no current version
      max_inputs: 4
      steps: [...]
    jobs:
      idx_g0_j0: [idx_g0_initial_chunk0, idx_g0_initial_chunk1, idx_g0_initial_chunk2]
      ...
      idx_g0_merge: [merge]

The fingerprint holds the input files the plan was made from: the definition, its shard files, layout.yaml, the sample lists and the --cluster file. apply refuses the plan when one of them changed, or when it was made by another kmhelpers version.

Report - BUILD_DIR/logs/kmhelpers_plan_<timestamp>.yaml: per shard and part, the build parameters (with where the partition count comes from), the kmtricks runs and chunks planned, the merge steps and their expected memory, and the scripts; plus the limits the sizing used, the host and the SLURM job. See build - Report.

Offline mode - use --offline to skip local path validation when generating scripts destined for another machine.

Filtering - --shard selects shards (all by default) by name or glob pattern: --shard 'idx_g0_*' selects every shard of group 0. A pattern that matches no shard is a warning; only no match at all is an error. The plan then holds only these shards.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text: A job is what apply --task <job> and a SLURM array task run. With --chunks-per-job 0 (default), a shard is one job, named after it: its chunks one after the other, then its merge. With --chunks-per-job N, a shard of more than N chunks gets ceil(chunks / N) jobs <shard>_j<k> of up to N chunks, which can run at the same time on several nodes, then <shard>_merge, which runs once they are all done.

docs.title: Cluster
docs.text:
--cluster FILE sizes the plan from the resources of the jobs that will run it, and writes the files submitting them, to BUILD_DIR/assets/SESSION/<type>/. type is required and selects the scheduler: only slurm for now; another type is refused before anything is planned or written.

type: slurm
partition: compute
time: 2-00:00:00
exclude: [node01]
max_parallel: 8                 # build array tasks running at once
output: logs/slurm/%x_%A_%a.out # relative to BUILD_DIR
setup: |                        # run before kmhelpers in every job
  export PATH=/path/to/kmhelpers/.env/bin:$PATH
extra: []                       # other sbatch options, as is
jobs:                           # resources per kind of job
  build: {cpus: 24, mem: 120G}
  merge: {cpus: 24, mem: 120G}
  check: {cpus: 1, mem: 4G, time: "1:00:00"}
limits: {files: 131072, maps: 65530}   # optional, see below
  • Keys under jobs.<kind> (partition, time, exclude, account, qos, constraint, cpus, mem, extra) override the top-level ones for that kind of job. Unknown keys are an error.
  • Chunks are sized from jobs.build (threads = cpus, RAM = mem x --safety-margin), merges from jobs.merge. --limits with --cluster is an error.
  • limits.files and limits.maps are node settings, not part of an allocation: without them, they are detected on the node plan runs on. Set them when the compute nodes differ: files is the hard open-files limit (ulimit -Hn; kmhelpers and its scripts raise the soft limit to it), maps is vm.max_map_count. Read them on a compute node with srun -p <partition> -c 1 --mem=1G -t 5 bash -c 'ulimit -Hn; cat /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count'.

plan writes BUILD_DIR/assets/SESSION/slurm/:

File Runs jobs.txt the build jobs, one per line build.sbatch an array task: one build job (apply --task) merge.sbatch one merge job (apply --task <shard>_merge) finish.sbatch after every job (afterany): manage check of the registry when nothing is pending, then apply --status (writes progress.yaml, mails it with build --notify); fails when the build is not done submit.sh submits the jobs apply --pending lists: the build array (%max_parallel, split at the cluster MaxArraySize), each merge job after the array tasks of its own shard, then the finish job. Safe to run again: only what is not done is submitted, never a job still queued or running submitted.tsv written by submit.sh: each job of the plan and its SLURM id, read by apply --status

Merge and finish jobs are cancelled when a job they wait on fails (--kill-on-invalid-dep=yes): nothing stays pending forever, and the finish job reports the failure. build --hpc plans and submits in one command, and takes --notify.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Plan a definition file
kmhelpers plan coli_db -o coli_build/

# Plan every shard of group 0 (glob pattern)
kmhelpers plan coli_db -o coli_build/ --sh 'coli_g0_*'

# Jobs of up to 4 chunks
kmhelpers plan coli_db -o coli_build/ --chunks-per-job 4

# Size the plan for the SLURM jobs of cluster.yaml, then submit them
kmhelpers plan coli_db -o coli_build/ --cluster cluster.yaml
bash coli_build/assets/initial/slurm/submit.sh

# Skip path validation (for exporting scripts)
kmhelpers plan coli_db -o coli_build/ --offline

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• apply - run the plan
  • build - run plan then apply in a single command
  • compose - generate index definition files

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Analyse a JSONL sample manifest produced by list and produce a Bloom-filter span profile.

USAGE

kmhelpers profile [OPTIONS] LIST_OUTPUT
Argument Description LIST_OUTPUT JSONL sample manifest produced by list (required) -o, --output DIR Output directory for results (required) -g, --group N Partition Bloom Filters into N storage-balanced groups and overlay on plot; 0 chooses N (default: 0), see profile - Grouping -b, --base FLOAT Base for span bucket boundaries (default: 1.1); use values like 1.1 or 2.0 to widen or narrow bucket granularity

I/O

Input: JSONL sample manifest produced by list Output: profile.yaml, groups.png in output directory (-o)

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description --fp, --false-positive-rate FLOAT Target Bloom-filter false-positive rate (default: 0.25) --auto-group-samples N With -g 0: start from one group per N samples (default: 1000, env: KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_SAMPLES) --auto-group-max N With -g 0: at most N groups (default: 20, env: KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_MAX) --auto-group-min-gain F With -g 0: storage fraction a further group must save to be added (default: 0.2, env: KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_MIN_GAIN) --auto-group-single-max SIZE With -g 0: keep one group when it takes at most SIZE (e.g. 4GB), compared with the presence/absence sizes of the profile; 0 for no such size (default: none, env: KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_SINGLE_MAX) --ngp, --no-grouping One group, no grouping strategy: every sample gets the Bloom filter of the largest one; not with -g N

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text: File Description profile.yaml Natural distribution and storage-balanced grouped profile(s) groups.png Span combination analysis plots

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A span is an integer s = floor(log_base(n)), where n is the number of distinct \(k\)-mers in a sample and base controls bucket granularity (-b, default: 1.1; the figure below uses base 2). It identifies the Bloom-filter size class required to index that sample at the target false-positive rate.

The figure above illustrates span assignment for five samples: each sample is placed on the k-mer count axis and falls into the bucket delimited by consecutive powers of the base. Here, samples whose k-mer count falls between \(2^{15}\) and \(2^{16}\) are assigned to Span 15.

A span profile is the distribution of samples across spans, together with candidate groupings of those spans into sub-indices. Fewer spans means fewer index files opened at query time, which improves query performance on I/O-bound storage.

profile reads \(k\)-mer counts from a JSONL file produced by list, assigns each sample to its span, and writes a CSV summary, a profile YAML, and a distribution plot to the output directory. Samples without a kmer_count field are skipped.

False-positive rate - a higher rate reduces Bloom-filter size and therefore disk footprint. At query time the findere algorithm compensates by querying \((k+z)\)-mers, reducing the effective FP rate to \(p^z\). Recommended: build with --fp 0.25 (default), query with -z 6, giving \(0.25^6 \approx 0.024\,\%\) effective FP rate.

Grouping - use -g N to merge spans into N storage-balanced sub-indices. Fewer sub-indices reduce the number of partition files opened per query. The grouping is overlaid on the distribution plot for visual inspection.

With -g 0 (default), profile chooses N:

  1. with --auto-group-single-max SIZE, it keeps one group when one group takes at most SIZE: a small index is not worth several sub-indexes, whatever they save in proportion (no such size by default; design sets 4 GB of built index);
  2. it starts from one group per 1000 samples (at least 1), so a group holds at most about 1000 samples;
  3. it then adds one group at a time while the new group reduces the total storage by at least 20%, and stops at the first one that does not;
  4. it never goes above 20 groups, nor above the number of spans.

Each group is one more sub-index to build, query and update, so a narrow distribution keeps few groups whatever its size. For example, 169 samples whose k-mer counts spread over two orders of magnitude start from 1 group (1.6 GB); a 2nd one saves 42% (0.95 GB), a 3rd only 18%, so they get 2 groups.

Sizes - the sizes in profile.yaml (disk_usage, total_size, bytes_per_sample) are for a presence/absence index, 1 bit per sample and Bloom-filter cell. An abundance index (design/compose --ab N) stores N bits per cell: multiply them by N, e.g. 208 MB becomes 624 MB with --ab 3. The factor is the same for every group, so it does not change the grouping chosen; compose counts it in its own estimates.

--auto-group-samples, --auto-group-max, --auto-group-min-gain and --auto-group-single-max (or their KMHELPERS_AUTO_GROUP_* environment variables) change these values. The chosen count is logged (Auto groups: N (… start …, max …, min gain …), or Auto groups: 1 (one group takes 760MB, at most 1.33GB)), and recorded with the values used under auto_group in profile.yaml, with single_size, the size of one group.

A single group is a valid choice on its own: queries read one row per k-mer and per sub-index, whose length does not depend on the Bloom filter size, so one sub-index is not slower to query; it only takes more space. -g N forces N groups, and --no-grouping skips the grouping strategy altogether: one group, sized for the largest sample (grouping: none in profile.yaml).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Profile with default settings
kmhelpers profile samples.jsonl -o ./profile_output

# Use a stricter false-positive rate
kmhelpers profile samples.jsonl -o ./profile_output --fp 0.05

# Let profile choose the number of span groups (default)
kmhelpers profile samples.jsonl -o ./profile_output -g 0

# Force a specific number of span groups
kmhelpers profile samples.jsonl -o ./profile_output -g 3

# Use a finer bucket granularity
kmhelpers profile samples.jsonl -o ./profile_output -b 1.5

docs.text:
• list - produce the JSONL input file
  • compose - use the JSONL from list and a profile to compose index definitions

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Query indices with FASTA/FASTQ sequences.

USAGE

kmhelpers query [OPTIONS] QUERY_FILES...
Argument Description QUERY_FILES... FASTA/FASTQ file(s), directories, or - for stdin (required) -r, --registry-path DIR Path to kmindex registry (default: .) -o, --output-dir DIR Output directory for results (required)

I/O

Input: FASTA/FASTQ file(s), kmindex registry (-r) Output: per query file in the output directory (-o): results.<format> (TSV by default), sequence_stats.tsv and sample_stats.tsv, the raw kmindex results in kmindex_output/, and optionally a report (--export)

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text: Option Description --sh, --shard TEXT Shards to query, as names or glob patterns (repeatable or comma-separated, e.g. 'idx_g0_*'; default: all) -t, --threads INT Number of threads (default: 1) -z, --zvalue INT Z-value for findere algorithm to filter false positives (default: 6) --thr, --threshold FLOAT Score threshold for filtering results (default: 0.05) --bq, --batch-query Treat all sequences across all query files as a single batched query -s, --single-query NAME Name for the single batched query -c, --compressed Index is compressed (forces sub parallelization) -f, --format TEXT Data format: tsv (default), json, yaml, or none to keep only the raw kmindex results. md and html are deprecated, they map to -f tsv --export <fmt> -x, --export TEXT Also write a human report: md or html. Not available with -f none --vec Also collect the per-k-mer presence/absence vector, not just the coverage ratio --page-size INT --export: sequences per detail page, a single file up to this count, 0 disables paging (default: 100) --top INT --export: best samples listed per sequence (default: 100) --no-stats Do not write sequence_stats.tsv and sample_stats.tsv -p, --print Print the data format to console instead of results.<format>, a report is still written to files --tms, --timestamp Append timestamp suffix to output directory to avoid overwriting -e, --existing TEXT Conflict resolution: skip (default), fail, delete, new-name --par, --parallel TEXT Parallelization strategy: seq (by sequence, default) or sub (by sub-index)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Searches one or more kmindex indices for sequences from FASTA/FASTQ files. Directories are scanned recursively. Pass - to read from stdin.

Each value in the output is the fraction of query k-mers found in that sample. Results below --threshold are filtered out.

Batch mode - use --batch-query to treat all sequences across all query files as a single query, or --single-query NAME to assign them a specific identifier.

Parallelization - seq parallelises across sequences (default); sub parallelises across sub-indices (forced when --compressed is set).

Statistics - written unless --no-stats (or --print). sequence_stats.tsv holds one row per sequence, then a * row over all sequences where each sample counts once with its best score:

Column Meaning samples samples with a score >= --threshold perfect samples with a score of 1 perfect_pct perfect / samples, in % mean, median over the matching scores

sample_stats.tsv is the reverse view: one row per matched sample (unmatched samples are left out, an index can hold millions), then a * row where each sequence counts once with its best score over samples:

Column Meaning queries sequences with a score >= --threshold in this sample perfect sequences with a score of 1 perfect_pct perfect / queries, in % mean, median over the matching scores

Data and reports - -f sets the data format: complete, unpaged, meant for scripts. --export adds a human report next to it, so one run gives both. -f none writes no converted file, the raw results stay in kmindex_output/ (JSON lines).

md/html reports (--export) - built to stay readable with thousands of sequences and millions of samples. The main file holds the run information (date, runtime, kmindex version, registry, threshold, command), the overall statistics, a short guide, and one line per sequence with its statistics and a link to its details. Each detail section lists the --top best samples of the sequence with their score. Up to --page-size sequences, everything is in results.md / results.html. Above, the main file is README.md / index.html and the details go to details/page_NNN.<format>, --page-size sequences per page. Statistics always use every match, --top only caps what is listed. All matches stay in kmindex_output/.

results/query/
  index.html
  sequence_stats.tsv
  sample_stats.tsv
  details/page_001.html
  details/page_002.html
  kmindex_output/

Presence vector - by default kmindex reports one coverage ratio R per sample:

{"index":"idx_0","query":"q0","samples":{"sample_0":0.69}}

With --vec it reports the per-k-mer presence vector P as well, R being its mean:

{"index":"idx_0","query":"q0","samples":{"sample_0":{"P":[1,1,0,...],"R":0.69}}}

The score matrix is identical either way. --vec adds, per (query, sample), the coverage stats n_kmers, covered, longest_run (longest stretch of consecutive k-mers found) and gaps (number of missing stretches), which tell a uniformly diluted match apart from one concentrated on a sub-region:

Format Where the vector data goes tsv coverage.tsv beside results.tsv, one row per (query, sample), P in a runs column md Coverage column with a text track (+ found, ~ partial, - missing) in each detail table html Coverage column with a colored track showing where the query is covered json stats plus P run-length encoded as [[value, count], ...] yaml stats plus the same P encoding, kept on one line

In the P encoding each pair is a run of consecutive k-mers, 1 present and 0 absent. For example [[1, 557], [0, 597], [1, 507]] means 557 k-mers found, then 597 missing, then 507 found.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Single query file against one index
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results query.fa

# Multiple query files with threading
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -t 4 -o results q1.fa q2.fa

# Query multiple indices
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 --sh idx2 -o results query.fa

# Read from stdin
cat query.fa | kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results -

# Scan a directory recursively
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results ./queries_dir/

# Treat all sequences as one batch query
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 --single-query batch1 -o results multi.fa

# Score threshold filtering
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results --thr 0.1 query.fa

# TSV data plus an HTML report
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results -f tsv --export html query.fa

# Raw kmindex results only
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results -f none query.fa

# Paged HTML report for many reads: 500 reads per page, 20 best samples each
kmhelpers query -r ./registry -o results -x html --page-size 500 --top 20 reads.fq.gz

# Per-k-mer coverage track in the HTML report
kmhelpers query -r ./registry --sh idx1 -o results -x html --vec query.fa

docs.title: From sample files to an index
docs.text:
design decides how the index is organized, from the sizes of the samples; build decides how to build it on this machine (or a cluster), then builds it. design runs three commands and build two, which can also be run one by one (see the step-by-step tutorial).

flowchart TD
    F["sample files"] -->|"list: count k-mers"| L["sample list<br/>(k-mers per sample)"]
    L -->|"profile: size classes"| PR["spans, then groups"]
    PR -->|"compose: index definition"| C["shards, session, layout"]
    C -->|"plan: decide the build"| PL["parts, chunks, jobs<br/>plan.yaml + scripts"]
    PL -->|"apply: kmtricks, one run per chunk"| R["runs"]
    R -->|"apply: merge, publish"| I["index: one folder per shard<br/>+ index.json"]

    subgraph design
        L
        PR
        C
    end
    subgraph build
        PL
        R
    end
  1. list counts the k-mers of each sample (K-mer counting).
  2. profile sorts the samples into spans by k-mer count, then merges consecutive spans into groups, balancing storage (profile).
  3. compose writes the index definition: the shards of each group, the samples this session adds to each shard, and the layout, kept for later updates.
  4. plan takes every build decision from the resources available: partitions, threads, whether a part is built in one run or in chunks, how chunks are merged, and the jobs. It builds nothing (plan).
  5. apply runs the plan: each chunk is one kmtricks run; the runs of a shard are merged, then published into the index, and checked (apply).

docs.title: Why shards and chunks
docs.text:
Both cut the samples into smaller sets, for different reasons:

Shard Chunk what a slice of a group, kept in the index a slice of the samples of one build, merged afterwards why keep each index of the samples bounded, as the index grows fit one kmtricks run in the open-files and memory limits of a machine decided by design (--sb), once for the life of the index plan (--cb, the resources), at each build visible in the index yes: one folder per shard no: only its shard is

See compose - Sharding and build - Shards and chunks.

docs.title: On a cluster
docs.text:
With --hpc cluster.yaml, plan sizes the build for the jobs of a SLURM cluster, and the jobs run the plan: chunks on several nodes at once, then one merge per shard. See build - On a cluster.

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as you
    participant B as build
    participant SL as SLURM
    participant A as array
    participant M as merge
    participant F as finish
    U->>B: --hpc cluster.yaml
    B->>B: plan:<br/>chunks, jobs
    B->>SL: submit
    B-->>U: submitted
    SL->>A: one task per job<br/>(several nodes)
    A->>A: build chunks<br/>(kmtricks)
    SL->>M: once its shard's<br/>jobs are done
    M->>M: merge,<br/>publish shard
    SL->>F: once every<br/>job has ended
    F->>F: check index,<br/>progress.yaml
    F-->>U: mail (--notify)
    Note over U,F: follow it: apply --status --sp

A failed job cancels the jobs waiting on it, and the finish job reports it; running the same build command again submits only what is not done.

docs.title: Updating an index
docs.text:
An update is a new session: its samples are added to the shards of the existing layout, so that the index keeps its groups, Bloom filter sizes and partitions.

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as you
    participant D as design
    participant B as build
    participant S as coli_g0
    U->>D: new samples<br/>-s update
    D->>D: each sample to its<br/>shard (layout)
    U->>B: -s update
    B->>B: build the new<br/>samples
    B->>B: merge with the<br/>current coli_g0
    Note over S: still queryable
    B->>S: swap in the<br/>merged version
    B->>B: check, delete the<br/>previous version

The swap takes a second or so; until then, queries see the previous version. An interrupted update is finished by running the same command again. See build - Updating an index and the update tutorial.

docs.title: K-mer counting
docs.text:
kmhelpers needs the k-mer count of each sample: it sets the size of the sample's Bloom filter, and places it in a span and a group (see How an index is built). list counts them with ntCard.

What is counted depends on the data type (--dt, list, design):

--dt Counted Why assembled (default) distinct k-mers assemblies are already corrected: every k-mer is genuine unassembled (raw reads) solid k-mers: those seen at least twice a k-mer seen once is most likely a sequencing error

Counts from elsewhere - the counts can come with the samples instead: a sample list (plain text or YAML) can give each sample its kmer_count, and list then does not count it (see list - Input formats). A JSONL sample list with the counts can also be given directly to design, which then skips list. Counting nothing at all: list --no-count.

Raw reads: the k-mer ratio

The sample list also keeps every k-mer occurrence (kmer_total). Building raw reads needs memory for all occurrences before the errors are dropped, so their ratio to the count sizes the build (see compose).

docs.title: What an index answers
docs.text:
For each k-mer of a query, an index tells which samples contain it. A query sequence gets one score per sample: the fraction of its k-mers found in that sample (1 when they all are). An abundance index (design --ab N) also stores how often each k-mer occurs, as a class from 0 to 2^N - 1, and reports that class instead.

Each sample is stored as a Bloom filter: a compact bit array that can answer "present" wrongly, at a known rate (--fp), but never "absent" wrongly. See the Glossary for the terms used below.

docs.title: Two ways of splitting
docs.text:
An index is a table: one column per sample, one row per Bloom filter position. kmhelpers splits it two ways:

  • by samples (columns): samples of similar sizes are grouped, and each group is stored as one or more shards. A shard is a complete index of its samples: it is built, queried and updated on its own.
  • by k-mers (rows): inside each shard, k-mers are spread over partitions by their minimizer, one file per partition. A query only reads the partitions its k-mers fall into.
flowchart TB
    I["index: coli_build/<br/>index.json lists the shards"]
    I --> S0["shard coli_g0<br/>small samples"]
    I --> S1["shard coli_g1<br/>large samples"]
    S0 --> P00["partition 0<br/>matrix_0.cmbf"]
    S0 --> P01["partition 1<br/>matrix_1.cmbf"]
    S0 --> P0N["..."]
    S1 --> P10["partition 0<br/>matrix_0.cmbf"]
    S1 --> P11["partition 1<br/>matrix_1.cmbf"]
    S1 --> P1N["..."]

The two splits are independent: every shard has all its partitions, and every partition holds all the samples of its shard. Grouping saves space (small samples do not get the Bloom filter size of the large ones); partitions keep each file, and each build step, a manageable size. See Choosing groups and partitions.

docs.title: On disk
docs.text:
The index directory (BUILD_DIR, build -o, query -r) is a kmindex registry:

coli_build/
├── index.json          the shards, and their parameters
├── coli_g0/            one shard, in place
│   ├── matrices/       one file per partition: matrix_0.cmbf, matrix_1.cmbf, ...
│   └── ...             kmtricks metadata (hashing, sample list)
├── coli_g1/
├── assets/<session>/   the plan of each session (scripts, plan.yaml)
├── logs/               build reports and logs
└── work/               temporary, only while a session is being built

Each shard is a folder of BUILD_DIR, kept at the same place for the whole life of the index: an update replaces its content, not its path.

index.json 
{
  "index": {
    "coli_g0": {
      "smer_size": 25,
      "minim_size": 10,
      "nb_partitions": 4,
      "bloom_size": 31404032,
      "bw": 1,
      "nb_samples": 5,
      "samples": ["GCA_000780515_1_ASM78051v1_genomic_fna", "..."]
    }
  }
}

smer_size is the k-mer size, minim_size the minimizer size, bw the bits per sample and k-mer (1 for presence/absence, N for --ab N).

docs.title: A query
docs.text:
kmhelpers query wraps kmindex query: it prepares the query files, runs kmindex on the index, then gathers its results into tables.

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as you
    participant Q as kmhelpers
    participant K as kmindex
    participant S as shards
    U->>Q: query.fa<br/>-r coli_build/
    Q->>Q: find the files,<br/>decompress if needed
    Q->>K: kmindex query
    K->>K: k-mers of<br/>each sequence
    loop each shard, in turn
        K->>S: look up the k-mers
        S-->>K: bits of every sample<br/>(only the partitions hit)
        K->>K: score<br/>per sample
    end
    K-->>Q: one result file<br/>per shard
    Q-->>U: results/: tables<br/>and statistics

Query time grows with the number of shards (each is read in turn), with the number of query k-mers, and with the samples of each shard (a row holds a bit for every sample). See query for the options (-z, --threshold, formats).

docs.title: Compression
docs.text: The partition files (matrices/*.cmbf) are stored uncompressed by default. compress recompresses them in place (matrices/blocks*), optionally reordering the sample columns first for a better ratio; queries then take --compressed.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The words used across this documentation, with the names they get in the E. coli tutorial.

docs.title: Sequences
docs.text: Term Meaning k-mer a substring of length k of a sequence (-k, default 25) solid k-mer a k-mer seen at least twice: in raw reads, a k-mer seen once is likely a sequencing error (see K-mer counting) minimizer the smallest sub-word of a k-mer, by a hash order; k-mers sharing a minimizer are stored together, in the same partition Bloom filter a compact bit array telling whether a k-mer belongs to a sample; it can answer "yes" wrongly (a false positive), never "no" wrongly false-positive rate how often a Bloom filter answers "yes" wrongly, set at design (--fp, default 0.25); queries lower it to about fp^z by looking up longer words (query -z, default 6)

docs.title: The index
docs.text:
An index is split two ways: its samples are spread over shards, and inside each shard its k-mers are spread over partitions.

Term Meaning In the tutorial Set by sample one input: a sequence file, or the mate files of one run GCA_000780515... the input of design span a size class of samples, by k-mer count: samples of one span get Bloom filters of the same size -b (base, default 1.1) group consecutive spans stored together, with the Bloom filter size of their largest span coli_g0, coli_g1 -g (0: chosen, see profile) shard the samples of a group, or a slice of them when the group is large: stored, queried and updated as one unit. Without sharding, a group is one shard coli_g0 (with a shard budget: coli_g0_p0, coli_g0_p1, ...) --sb (0: no sharding, see compose) partition a slice of the k-mers of a shard, by minimizer: one file per partition in each shard. A query reads only the partitions its k-mers fall into coli_g0/matrices/matrix_3.cmbf chosen at the first build, then fixed (-P to set it) sub-index one kmindex index: a shard, or a chunk before it is merged into its shard index the directory holding every shard of an index, and index.json listing them: the registry (BUILD_DIR) coli_build/ build -o, read by query -r 
flowchart TB
    S["samples"] -->|"by k-mer count (-b)"| SP["spans"]
    SP -->|"consecutive spans (-g)"| G["groups"]
    G -->|"split if large (--sb)"| SH["shards"]
    SH -->|"k-mers by minimizer (-P)"| P["partitions<br/>one file each"]

docs.title: Building and updating
docs.text:
Term Meaning In the tutorial Set by design directory what design writes: the sample list, the profile, and the index definition coli_db/ design -o layout the fixed choices of an index (groups, shards, Bloom sizes, partitions), reused by every update coli_db/compose/coli/layout.yaml the first design session one set of samples added to an index: the first one, then each update initial, update -s part (task) the samples a session adds to one shard coli_g0_initial, coli_g0_update compose chunk one kmtricks run building some samples of a part; a part too large for one run is built in chunks, then merged coli_g0_initial_chunk3 --cb, the open-files limit (see build) plan every build decision, and the scripts running them, written before anything is built coli_build/assets/initial/plan.yaml plan job the unit apply runs, and a SLURM task: a shard, some of its chunks, or its merge coli_g0, coli_g0_j1, coli_g0_merge --chunks-per-job (see plan) step one kmtricks run or one merge, with its status (SUCCESS, FAILED, ...) chunk3, merge see apply

See How an index is structured and How an index is built.

docs.title: Choosing groups and partitions
docs.text:
The layout of an index rests on two settings (see the Glossary):

  • groups (-g, design, profile): how many sets of samples of similar sizes. Each group gets the Bloom filter size of its largest samples, and is stored as one shard (or several, with a shard budget). By default (-g 0) the number is chosen: groups are added while each saves at least 20% of the storage; with design, an index of at most 4 GB keeps one group (see profile - Grouping).
  • partitions (-P, hidden option of design and compose): how many files the k-mers of each shard are spread over. Best left unset: the first plan sizes it from the resources, then it is fixed for the life of the index.
Goal Groups (-g) Partitions (-P) Why Faster queries fewer fewer each shard is read in turn; fewer files per query Less storage more Bloom filter sizes fit the samples more tightly: a small sample in a group of large ones gets their large filter Lower build RAM more more less held at once by one build; usually handled by plan (partitions, threads, chunks)

Check the storage of each choice of groups in profile.yaml and groups.png (from profile), and set -g explicitly when the automatic choice does not fit your use.

docs.title: Contributing to kmhelpers
docs.text:
First off, thanks for taking the time to contribute! ❤️

All types of contributions are encouraged and valued. See the Table of Contents for different ways to help and details about how this project handles them. Please make sure to read the relevant section before making your contribution. It will make it a lot easier for us maintainers and smooth out the experience for all involved. The community looks forward to your contributions. 🎉

And if you like the project, but just don't have time to contribute, that's fine. There are other easy ways to support the project and show your appreciation, which we would also be very happy about: - Star the project - Mention the project at local meetups and tell your friends/colleagues - Refer this project in your project's readme

docs.title: I Have a Question
docs.text:
If you want to ask a question, we assume that you have read the available Documentation.

Before you ask a question, it is best to search for existing Issues that might help you. In case you have found a suitable issue and still need clarification, you can write your question in this issue. It is also advisable to search the internet for answers first.

If you then still feel the need to ask a question and need clarification, we recommend the following:

  • Open an Issue.
  • Provide as much context as you can about what you're running into.
  • Provide your OS, Python version, conda version, kmhelpers version, and kmindex version, depending on what seems relevant.

We will then take care of the issue as soon as possible.

docs.title: Legal Notice
docs.text: When contributing to this project, you must agree that you have authored 100% of the content, that you have the necessary rights to the content and that the content you contribute may be provided under the project license (GPL-3.0-only).

docs.title: Before Submitting a Bug Report
docs.text:
A good bug report shouldn't leave others needing to chase you up for more information. Therefore, we ask you to investigate carefully, collect information and describe the issue in detail in your report. Please complete the following steps in advance to help us fix any potential bug as fast as possible.

  • Make sure that you are using the latest version.
  • Determine if your bug is really a bug and not an error on your side e.g. using an incompatible environment or version of kmindex (Make sure that you have read the documentation. If you are looking for support, you might want to check this section).
  • Also make sure to search the internet (including Stack Overflow) to see if users outside of the GitHub community have discussed the issue.
  • Collect information about the bug:
  • Stack trace (Traceback)
  • OS, platform and version (Linux x86_64, macOS Intel, macOS Apple Silicon)
  • Python version and conda environment details (conda info, pip show pykmhelpers)
  • kmhelpers version (kh --version)
  • Version of kmindex, kmtricks, and ntCard (kmindex --version, kmtricks --version, ntcard --version)
  • Possibly your input (JSONL sample list, YAML config) and the output
  • If kmhelpers crashed, attach the dump file (kmhelpers_<timestamp>.dump) written to your working directory
  • Can you reliably reproduce the issue? And can you also reproduce it with older versions?

docs.title: How Do I Submit a Good Bug Report?
docs.text:
You must never report security related issues, vulnerabilities or bugs including sensitive information to the issue tracker, or elsewhere in public. Instead sensitive bugs must be sent by email to kmhelpers@groupes.renater.fr.

We use GitHub issues to track bugs and errors. If you run into an issue with the project:

  • Open an Issue. (Since we can't be sure at this point whether it is a bug or not, we ask you not to talk about a bug yet and not to label the issue.)
  • Explain the behavior you would expect and the actual behavior.
  • Please provide as much context as possible and describe the reproduction steps that someone else can follow to recreate the issue on their own. This usually includes the command you ran and the relevant input files or configuration. For good bug reports you should isolate the problem and create a reduced test case.
  • Provide the information you collected in the previous section.

Once it's filed:

  • The project team will label the issue accordingly.
  • A team member will try to reproduce the issue with your provided steps. If there are no reproduction steps or no obvious way to reproduce the issue, the team will ask you for those steps and mark the issue as needs-repro. Bugs with the needs-repro tag will not be addressed until they are reproduced.
  • If the team is able to reproduce the issue, it will be marked needs-fix, as well as possibly other tags (such as critical), and the issue will be left to be implemented by someone.

docs.title: Suggesting Enhancements
docs.text: This section guides you through submitting an enhancement suggestion for kmhelpers, including completely new features and minor improvements to existing functionality. Following these guidelines will help maintainers and the community to understand your suggestion and find related suggestions.

docs.title: Before Submitting an Enhancement
docs.text:
• Make sure that you are using the latest version.
  • Read the documentation carefully and find out if the functionality is already covered, maybe by an individual configuration.
  • Perform a search to see if the enhancement has already been suggested. If it has, add a comment to the existing issue instead of opening a new one.
  • Find out whether your idea fits with the scope and aims of the project. It's up to you to make a strong case to convince the project's developers of the merits of this feature. Keep in mind that we want features that will be useful to the majority of our users and not just a small subset.

docs.title: How Do I Submit a Good Enhancement Suggestion?
docs.text:
Enhancement suggestions are tracked as GitHub issues.

  • Use a clear and descriptive title for the issue to identify the suggestion.
  • Provide a step-by-step description of the suggested enhancement in as many details as possible.
  • Describe the current behavior and explain which behavior you expected to see instead and why. At this point you can also tell which alternatives do not work for you.
  • Explain why this enhancement would be useful to most kmhelpers users. You may also want to point out other projects that solved it better and which could serve as inspiration.

docs.title: Setting up the development environment
docs.text:
1. Fork and clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/kmhelpers
cd kmhelpers

  2. Create the conda environment and install kmhelpers in editable mode: 

    conda env create -f conda/environment.yml -p ./.env
conda activate ./.env
pip install -e ".[dev]"

  3. Run the test suite to verify everything is working: 

    pytest

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
• Create a feature branch from main: git checkout -b feature/my-feature
  • Make your changes and add tests under pykmhelpers/tests/
  • Ensure all checks pass before opening a pull request: 
    black pykmhelpers          # format
flake8 pykmhelpers         # lint
mypy pykmhelpers           # type-check
pytest                     # tests
  • Open a pull request against the main branch.

docs.title: Improving The Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is built with MkDocs Material and hosted at https://sebllns.github.io/kmhelpers/.

To preview the docs locally:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve

Source files live under docs/. Please keep the documentation consistent with any code changes you make.

docs.title: Code Style
docs.text:
• Formatter: Black with line-length = 88. Run black pykmhelpers before committing.
  • Linter: Flake8. Run flake8 pykmhelpers before committing.
  • Type hints: encouraged. Run mypy pykmhelpers to check.
  • Import order: isort with the black profile.

docs.title: Commit Messages
docs.text:
• Use the imperative mood: "Add feature", not "Added feature".
  • Keep the subject line under 72 characters.
  • Reference related issues where applicable: Fix #42 — ….
  • Notable changes should be reflected in CHANGELOG.md under the relevant version section.

docs.title: Join The Project Team
docs.text: If you are interested in becoming a regular contributor or maintainer, reach out by opening an issue or contacting us at kmhelpers@groupes.renater.fr.
